::: {.callout-note .objectives title="Learning objectives"}
* To learn about the categorical data class - *factors* 
* To understand more complex R data structures like data frames, lists etc
:::


# Factors

* **Factor** -- R's vector class for **categorical** data; sex, tumour stage etc
* Possible values are limited to a fixed set of **levels**
* Matters for plotting and stats
* **Gotcha:** look like character vectors, stored as integers -- be careful
  converting

## Creating a factor

* `factor()` on a character vector

```{r}
#| label: factor_create
x <- c("orange", "apple", "apple", "orange")
x
fruit <- factor(x) # convert vector x into a factor
fruit
class(x)
class(fruit)
```

## Factors store the categories as "levels" 

* `levels()` -- the only valid values

```{r}
#| label: factor_levels
levels(fruit)
```

* Assigning a value that is not a level gives `NA` -- silently

```{r}
#| label: factor_invalid_value
fruit[1] <- "apple"
fruit[2] <- "banana"
fruit
```

## The values of the factors are actually stored as integers

* Printed as labels, stored as integers `1, 2, 3 ...` -- compact storage for
  large categorical data
* `as.numeric()` exposes the integers

```{r}
#| label: factor_stored_as_integers
x <- c("low", "high", "medium", "high", "low", "medium", "high")
response <- factor(x)
as.numeric(x)
response
as.numeric(response)
```

## We can change the order of the levels

* Level order drives plotting order, and the first level is the **reference**
  level in models
* Default is alphabetical -- here "high", "low", "medium"; we want
  "low", "medium", "high"
* Set with the `levels =` argument

```{r}
#| label: factor_specify_levels
response <- factor(x, levels = c("low", "medium", "high"))
response
```

## Converting factors to plain vector types

* `as.character()` -- original category labels
* `as.numeric()` -- level index, *not* the label

```{r}
#| label: factor_convert_to_vector
response
as.character(response)
as.numeric(response)
```

* **The classic gotcha** -- categories that look like numbers; `as.numeric()`
  returns level indices, not years

```{r}
#| label: factor_numeric_categories
x <- c(1987, 2002, 2019, 2004, 1983, 1982, 1999, 2004)
dateOfBirth <- factor(x)
dateOfBirth
as.character(dateOfBirth)
as.numeric(dateOfBirth)
```

* Fix -- two stages, via `as.character()` first

```{r}
#| label: factor_numeric_conversion_two_stage
dob <- as.character(dateOfBirth)
dob <- as.numeric(dob)
dob
age <- 2023 - dob
age
```

# Beyond the atomic vector - matrices, data.frames and lists

::: {.showimg}
![](./assets/imgs/shared/dataStructures.png)

Show **the R data structures diagram** here
:::

R has many data structures. These include:

- [x] atomic vector
- [ ] matrix
- [ ] data frame
- [ ] list

## Matrices 

* Matrix = 2D extension of the atomic vector; rows and columns are vectors
* All one data type, all the same length

```{r}
#| label: matrix_create
y <- matrix(data = 1:12, nrow = 4, ncol = 3)
y
class(y)
typeof(y)
```

* Two dimensions -- first rows, second columns
* dim(): Provides the dimensions of an object  
* nrow(): gives number of rows  
* ncol(): gives number of columns

```{r}
#| label: matrix_dimensions
dim(y)
nrow(y)
ncol(y)
```

* Subsetting syntax is `matrix[ rows , columns ]` -- both required

```{r}
#| label: matrix_single_value
y[1, 2]
```

* Omit an index to get a whole row or column

```{r}
#| label: matrix_row_and_column
y[1, ]
y[, 3]
```

* Vectors inside `[]` for multiple values

```{r}
#| label: matrix_multiple_values
y[c(1, 3), 2:3]
```

* **Coercion** -- one character value converts the whole matrix to character

```{r}
#| label: matrix_type_coercion
typeof(y)
y
y[2, 3]
y[2, 3] <- "A"
y
typeof(y)
```

## Lists

* **List** -- collection of any objects, mixed types, mixed lengths; can contain
  lists

```{r}
#| label: list_create
w <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
x <- 1:10
y <- c("a", "b", "c")
z <- matrix(1:12, nrow = 3, ncol = 4)

myList <- list(w, x, y, z)
myList
```

* Note the double square brackets in the printed output -- clue to the two
  operators:

1. `[]`: Standard subscript operator, works like in a vector. The output is
   still a list. 
2. `[[]]`: This operator can only take one index number at a time and the
   output will be the data structure for that element.

```{r}
#| label: list_single_bracket
length(myList)
myList[1]
myList[4]
myList[1:3]
```

* `myList[[1:3]]` errors -- one index only

```{r}
#| label: list_double_bracket
#| error: true
length(myList)
myList[[1]]
myList[[4]]
myList[[1:3]]
```

3. "$": to extract an element from a list by name.

```{r}
#| label: list_named_elements
namedList <- list(
    city = c("Kampala", "London", "Paris"),
    population = c(1.51, 8.8, 2.1)
)

namedList

namedList$city
namedList$population
names(namedList)
```

* Modify existing elements, or add new ones by naming them

```{r}
#| label: list_modify
namedList$city[2] <- "New York"
namedList$country <- c("Uganda", "USA", "France")
namedList
```

* Why they matter -- lists underlie the data frame, and statistical tests return
  their results as lists
* Demo: `t.test` on two samples from `rnorm()`

```{r}
#| label: set_seed
#| include: false
set.seed(101010)
```

```{r}
#| label: t_test_result_list
sample_1 <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 5, sd = 1)
sample_2 <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 7, sd = 1)

result <- t.test(x = sample_1, y = sample_2)

is.list(result)
result
names(result)
result$statistic
result$p.value
```

## Data frames

* Most common structure -- a table; each column its own data class, one class
  within a column
* Actually a **list of equal-length vectors**

```{r}
#| label: data_frame_create
dat <- data.frame(
    city = c("Kampala", "London", "Paris"),
    population = c(1.51, 8.8, 2.1)
)
dat
class(dat)
dim(dat)
```

* Built-in data sets -- list them with `data()`
* `iris`:

* data frame  
* 150 observations (rows)    
* 5 variables (columns)  
    * Sepal.Length  
    * Sepal.Width  
    * Petal.Length  
    * Petal.Width  
    * Species  

* Just use it by name -- no loading needed

```{r}
#| label: iris_first_use
head(iris)
```

```{r}
#| label: iris_help
#| eval: false
?iris # get help for iris data
```

* Fisher's data set -- of Fisher's exact test fame

* head(): Shows first 6 lines of a data frame  
* tail(): Shows first 6 lines of a data frame  
* View(): Shows data frame in excel like format  

```{r}
#| label: iris_head
head(iris)
```

```{r}
#| label: iris_tail
tail(iris)
```

```{r}
#| label: iris_view
#| eval: false
View(iris)
```

* It's a list, so `$` works for columns

```{r}
#| label: iris_column_by_name
names(iris)
iris$Petal.Width
```

* Column is a vector -- subset it further

```{r}
#| label: iris_column_subset
iris$Petal.Length[1:10]
```

* `[, ]` works as for matrices

```{r}
#| label: iris_rows_and_columns
iris[1:4, 1:3]
iris[c(1, 4, 7),  c(2, 4)]
```

* Names work as well as indices

```{r}
#| label: iris_subset_by_name
iris[c(1, 4, 7),  c("Sepal.Width", "Species" )]
```

* **Conditional subsetting** -- logical vector in the row position; do not forget
  the trailing comma

```{r}
#| label: iris_conditional_subset
iris[iris$Sepal.Length == 5, ]
```

* Combine conditions with `&` (and), `|` (or), `!` (not)

```{r}
#| label: iris_conditional_subset_multiple
iris[iris$Sepal.Length == 5 & iris$Species == "setosa", ]
```

* Flag that the syntax is unintuitive -- motivation for
  [tidyverse ](https://www.tidyverse.org/), next session

* dplyr: Makes working with data frames fun and easy  
* ggplot2: Creates beautiful plots with ease.

* **`summary()`**  is a very useful function that summarises each column in a data frame

```{r}
#| label: iris_summary
summary(iris)
```
